items.title: Single-family permits telegraph a weakened 2027 building pipeline
items.description: While October saw a blip in housing starts, the latest residential construction data from the U.S. Census Bureau shows a single-family construction market seeking rock bottom, with single-family permits hitting a nearly four-year low. National housing starts rose to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.309 million in October, up 9.9% from the revised September figure of 1.191 million and 2.8% above the same month last year (1.273 million). Most of that increase came from multifamily, where starts climbed 23.6% from September to an annualized rate of 445,000. Single-family starts came in at an annual rate of 864,000 in October, up 4.0% from September but down 3.2% from a year earlier, suggesting single-family construction lacks momentum. "Given monthly volatility, the three-month moving average provides a clearer signal, which fell to 859,000 units," according to a note by National Association of Home Builders Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington The future construction pipeline also looks soft. Single-family permits, a forward-looking indicator of where new home construction levels are headed, dropped 8.7% in October to an annual rate of 772,000, down from a revised 846,000 in September and 12.9% lower than a year ago. That marks the lowest level for single-family permits since January 2023. Total housing permits, including both multifamily and single-family, were 8.7% below the October 2025 rate of 1.418 million. “Permits point to a slowdown in single-family production ahead,” First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming said in a provided statement. “Since permits lead construction, the decline suggests builders are moving ahead with projects already in the pipeline, while authorizing fewer single-family homes for future construction.” The new data comes as homebuilder confidence fell to its lowest level in nearly 15 years in November, with affordability constraints and hesitant buyers weighing on the market. That buyer hesitancy is reflected in the latest new home sales figures, which show sales down 5.3% year over year in September and sales prices down roughly 4.0% to $400,400. Fleming pointed to weakening demand, higher costs and elevated mortgage rates as catalysts for a softening residential construction pipeline. “Prospective buyer traffic fell to its weakest level in 15 years, outside the start of the pandemic. Builders are using price cuts and incentives to reach buyers, while labor shortages and higher fuel costs are adding to the cost of building. That combination leaves builders cautious about adding production when affordability is already keeping many buyers on the sidelines,” he said. Homes under construction slip as completions lag The stock of homes under construction continues to move down from recent highs. Housing units under construction totaled 1.27 million in October, 3.0% below a year earlier. Single-family units under construction came to 581,000, down 2.5% year over year, while multifamily units in progress fell to 691,000, 3.5% lower than a year ago and well off the peak of more than 1 million reached in December 2023. Meanwhile, housing completions improved from September but remained negative year on year. Total completions reached an annual rate of 1.272 million in October, up 6.5% from September’s revised 1.194 million but 10.4% below the 1.419 million recorded in October 2025. Single-family completions came in at 900,000, down 10.7% compared to a year earlier, while multifamily completions in buildings with five or more units ran at 362,000, down 9.0% on the year. Regional trends Year to date, combined single-family and multifamily starts rose 3.8% in the Northeast and 0.2% in the South, while falling 0.7% in the Midwest and 6.7% in the West. Single-family construction declined across all four regions, signaling the strain high construction costs and affordability constraints are putting on homebuilders and prospective buyers. The permit data points in the same direction. Total permits are up 8.7% in the Northeast and 2.0% in the Midwest this year, but down 4.4% in the South and 2.5% in the West. With single-family permits lower in all four regions, the outlook for a slowing national construction pipeline looks even more likely. Zillow Senior Economist Kenny Lee noted that the slowdown in single-family starts and permits indicates that homebuilders may be preparing for a relatively weak spring selling season. “While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane,” Lee explained. Related More: Homebuilders Housing Starts

items.title: Newrez settles Washington state servicing case with $3 million payout
items.description: Newrez agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement broad mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) that the company engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices. The consent order, which stems from a multiyear servicing investigation, lands below the $4.175 million civil penalty sought earlier this year by DFI in a statement of charges, but it still represents a significant financial and operational hit for the nonbank servicer. Newrez does not admit or deny any wrongdoing under the agreement. A company spokesperson told HousingWire the company is “pleased to have resolved this matter.” “The underlying examination resulted in limited findings, most of which had already been addressed by Newrez. The agreement, which includes no admission of wrongdoing, credits Newrez for several investments made to enhance its operations. We remain committed to supporting homeowners and meeting the high standards they expect,” the spokesperson said. Under the order, Newrez must pay $2.5 million to DFI, plus at least $500,000 earmarked for consumer remediation and technology and system upgrades. The company also owes an investigation fee of $14,888.90 to cover the agency’s staff time. The case grew out of more than 125 consumer complaints to DFI, including allegations of unfair or deceptive acts or practices affecting at least 29 borrowers. Regulators also cited failures to maintain and service escrow accounts for at least 71 loans to Washington residents. Earlier charges alleged servicing breakdowns in Washington from 2021 to 2026. These included loan boarding errors that caused private mortgage insurance and escrow problems, misapplied payments, issues with escrow and force‑placed insurance , inaccurate information during foreclosure mediation, faulty statements, and overdue responses to both borrowers and the regulator. In addition to the monetary obligations, the consent order requires Newrez to undertake affirmative actions across its servicing platform. The company must tighten loan onboarding processes, overhaul core servicing functions, and improve controls over escrow and insurance handling, among other changes. Newrez has to demonstrate to DFI that these corrective actions are complete within 30 days of the order’s effective date. “Washington state mortgage servicing laws exist to ensure homeowners are treated fairly and that their loans are serviced properly,” DFI Director Charlie Clark said in a statement. “DFI will take action to hold mortgage servicers accountable and will order affirmative action needed to protect Washington homeowners.” Related More: NewRez Washington

items.title: Oklahoma City, OK, Struggles With Low Starter Home Availability Compared to Other Cities
items.description: A recent metro-by-metro analysis by Realtor.com® reveals where buyers can still find a starter home . For many would-be homeowners, these options have felt increasingly scarce as rising prices and climbing mortgage rates compound affordability challenges. Furthermore, research from economists supports this trend. Nationally, the share of starter homes in active inventory fell from 38.1% in August 2019 to 36.2% in August 2026. During that same period, starter home prices rose 30.8%, from roughly $260,000 to $340,000. As a result, some markets like Oklahoma City have experienced a downturn in available starter homes in recent years. Starter home availability declines in Oklahoma City A starter home is typically defined as a property priced at roughly 80% of a metro's median list price. This captures the relative affordability of homes at the lower end of a local market. These homes are generally smaller and less expensive, making them accessible to a first-time buyer or a household with an Income at or below the area median. In Oklahoma City, OK, the share of starter homes has seen a steady decline. The portion of these homes was 34.8% in 2019, which then decreased to 33.1% in 2022. As of 2026, the share has fallen further to 31.4%. Therefore, this represents a total decrease of 3.4 percentage points between 2019 and 2026. This trend indicates a shrinking market for entry-level homes in the area, presenting a challenge for new buyers. Renting remains the affordable option for now For those weighing the decision of renting or buying , current data suggests that renting is the more financially prudent choice for now. A July Rent Report from Realtor.com found that the cost of buying a starter home in the 50 largest metros was $858 higher per month than renting one. This 50.6% premium on homeownership makes renting the more affordable option across all 50 of the largest metros. In Oklahoma City, OK, this trend holds, offering a clear financial advantage to renters. The median rent for an apartment was $915 as of July 2026. Moreover, the local rental market has seen prices decrease by 1.50% year-over-year, making it an even more attractive alternative to purchasing a home with a significant down payment . items.title: Housing groups urge FHFA to delay condo reserve rule until 2028
items.description: Five housing and mortgage industry trade groups are asking the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to delay a planned increase in condominium association reserve requirements by one year, citing implementation challenges and potential financing disruptions. In a Nov. 19 letter sent to FHFA Director Bill Pulte , the organizations asked the agency to direct Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to postpone the changes from Jan. 4, 2027, to Jan. 4, 2028. The new requirement would increase the minimum reserve allocation for applicable condominium project reviews from 10% to 15% of annual budgeted assessment income. The letter was signed by the Community Associations Institute , Community Association Roundtable , Community Home Lenders of America ( CHLA ), Housing Policy Council and National Association of Mortgage Brokers ( NAMB ). The groups said they support adequately funded condominium reserves but argued that associations, lenders and homeowners need more time to prepare for the change. Some have asked for change before. In June, NAMB asked the FHFA to delay upcoming Fannie and Freddie condo review and insurance standards by 12 months. But Fannie Mae retired its limited review process for condominium projects on Aug. 3. "Condominium project eligibility has already declined following recent changes to project review requirements, including the elimination of Limited Review options," the groups wrote. Outlining their concerns The coalition identified three primary concerns with the planned increase, stating that "the change could have unintended consequences for condominium financing and housing availability." First, many condominium associations operate on annual budget cycles and cannot easily adjust their funding midyear. Some may also need updated reserve studies, board approvals or homeowner consultations before changing their funding practices. The groups also said questions remain about how the new requirement will apply to existing budgets, recently completed reserve studies, major capital improvement projects and alternative funding arrangements. Lenders, servicers and condo management companies will also need time to update their systems, underwriting procedures and project reviews. Second, the groups warned that associations unable to meet the higher reserve requirement or qualify under an alternative reserve study provision could lose eligibility for conventional financing through the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs). The groups raised concerns that this could reduce the pool of potential buyers, make it more difficult for existing homeowners to sell or refinance, and put pressure on condo resale values. The impact could be particularly pronounced in older buildings, smaller communities and associations with more "modest-income" homeowners, the letter stated. Projects that lose conventional financing eligibility could become more reliant on nonagency or portfolio loans, which may be more expensive or less readily available. Lastly, the coalition said higher reserve contributions could add to housing costs at a time when homeowners are already facing elevated mortgage payments, property taxes , insurance premiums, maintenance expenses and association fees. Fannie Mae has estimated that the higher reserve requirement could add an average of $13 to $14 per month to condominium owners' costs, but the actual increase would vary by association, according to the coalition. Its accompanying analysis illustrated how the additional five percentage points could affect homeowners if the entire increase were funded through regular assessments. As part of the proposed one-year extension, the coalition urged FHFA to convene industry stakeholders to evaluate the financial and operational effects of the change, clarify how existing reserve studies and funding arrangements will be treated, and develop transition provisions for associations working toward adequate reserve funding. "We believe that strengthening condominium financial health and maintaining housing affordability should be complementary objectives," the letter said. items.title: Senate committee advances Matt Jones’ nomination as FHA commissioner
items.description: Matt Jones’ nomination to serve as assistant secretary for housing at the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and as Federal Housing Administration (FHA) commissioner advanced in the Senate on Thursday, moving through committee on a narrow vote. The Senate Committee on Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs approved his nomination 13-11, sending it to the full Senate for consideration. Jones would permanently fill the vacancy left by Frank Cassidy in June and succeed Joseph Gormley , who has been serving in the role on an acting basis. Committee chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) said Jones’ mix of public- and private-sector experience is central to his support. According to Scott, housing affordability remains one of the biggest challenges facing families across America, but if confirmed, Jones “will play an important role in implementing the 21st Century Road to Housing Act and helping more families achieve the American dream of home ownership.” Jones currently serves as HUD’s deputy assistant secretary for single-family housing. He previously was associate vice president of government housing finance at the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), senior adviser for capital markets at A merifirst Home Mortgage , and senior counsel for the Senate’s Finance and Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs committees. The 13-11 vote reflected partisan divisions over the direction of federal housing policy and FHA’s role in addressing affordability and ownership gaps. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), the committee’s ranking member, voted against the nomination, saying Jones’ office has “cut resources for first-time homebuyers and proposed weak rules for keeping foreclosed homes in the hands of families instead of corporations.” “We should vote to make life more affordable for American families. But these nominees will do the opposite, accelerating the Trump administration 's disastrous economic policies,” Warren said. If confirmed, Jones would oversee FHA’s single-family, multifamily and health care mortgage insurance portfolios. FHA currently insures roughly $2 trillion in mortgages. The FHA’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels. The results have renewed industry pressure on FHA to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums to ease costs for first-time and lower-income borrowers. Jones would also inherit an agency that has seen a series of policy adjustments under HUD Secretary Scott Turner , including efforts to revise servicing standards and modernize technology infrastructure. MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said the trade group supports the nomination due to Jones’ “extensive mortgage industry experience, deep understanding of government housing finance, and leadership of FHA’s single-family operations.” “We urge the full Senate to confirm Matt Jones before the 119th Congress adjourns and look forward to working with him and HUD to continue modernizing FHA programs and to improve affordability for owning and renting a home,” Broeksmit said. items.title: Broker Action Coalition pushes for QM change on compensation cap
items.description: The Broker Action Coalition (BAC) is proposing a change to federal mortgage rules that would exclude lender-paid mortgage broker compensation from the Qualified Mortgage (QM) points-and-fees calculation, aligning its treatment with compensation paid to retail lenders' employee loan officers. In a white paper recently released by BAC , the coalition argues that the current rules create an uneven playing field between independent mortgage brokers and retail lenders, particularly on smaller-balance loans . Under the Ability-to-Repay/Qualified Mortgage rule, points and fees generally cannot exceed 3% of a loan amount for loans of $137,958 or more in 2026. Smaller loans are subject to graduated percentage and dollar limits. Currently, compensation paid by a wholesale lender to an independent mortgage broker counts toward that limit, while compensation paid by a retail lender to its own employee loan officer is excluded. The coalition argues that both types of compensation are often funded through the interest rate and are indistinguishable from the borrower's perspective. The difference can leave brokers with less room to cover other fees that count toward the cap, potentially causing otherwise qualifying loans to exceed the limit while losing QM status and its associated liability protections. The disparity is particularly pronounced on smaller loans, where the dollar limits leave less room for additional charges. The coalition said small-balance and rural loans are particularly vulnerable because fixed-dollar charges consume a larger share of the available cap. Small-dollar lending hurdles The white paper also points to a decline in small-dollar mortgage lending. The share of home purchase loans under $70,000 fell from more than 11% in 2011 to less than 4% in 2020, citing research from Pew Charitable Trusts , the Urban Institute and the Department of Housing and Urban Development . In rural and lower-cost markets, the group argues, the restrictions can make it harder for brokers to compete for loans that are already less financially attractive to originate. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau 's 2013 rulemaking established the distinction between employee and broker compensation. At the time, the bureau said including broker compensation in the calculation could help reduce the risk of mortgage brokers steering borrowers toward more expensive transactions. The coalition acknowledges that consumer protection concern but argues that subsequent regulations addressing loan originator compensation and steering have made the points-and-fees restriction a less targeted way to address the issue. Specifically, the group points to existing rules that prohibit loan originator compensation from varying based on a loan's interest rate or other terms, as well as a separate prohibition on steering borrowers toward transactions that provide greater compensation. The proposed reform would take two approaches: The primary proposal is a statutory amendment to the Truth in Lending Act that would exclude rate-funded creditor-to-broker compensation from the points-and-fees definition when it is paid under a compliant loan originator compensation agreement. The parallel regulatory proposal would ask the CFPB to amend Regulation Z to create the same exclusion. "The proposed reform would remove an inequitable regulatory constraint without changing the competitive forces that influence compensation today," the paper reads. "While individual brokerages may adjust their compensation arrangements, there is little evidence to suggest that the reform would materially diminish the wholesale channel 's overall pricing competitiveness." Avoiding circumvention Under the proposed language, the exclusion would apply only when compensation is funded through the interest rate, is not paid directly by the borrower or financed into the loan amount, and is established through a standing agreement between the creditor and broker that does not vary based on individual loan terms. The coalition said the proposed requirements would prevent brokers from adjusting compensation on individual loans to circumvent the cap. The change would leave the 3% limit and existing compensation and anti-steering rules intact, with borrower-paid compensation and other fees still subject to the cap. Data from two wholesale lenders representing $13.4 billion in combined 2026 production showed that loans with 2.75% broker compensation accounted for 14.53% of units and 12.41% of volume. BAC said the figures indicate most brokered loans close with lower compensation. The group also argued that the CFPB has authority under the Truth in Lending Act to make the change to preserve access to affordable mortgage credit. It cited the bureau's 2019 assessment of the Ability-to-Repay and Qualified Mortgage rule, which documented fee waivers and other challenges affecting smaller brokered loans. items.title: Anthropic's Record IPO Reverberates Across Data Center Sector
items.description: Anthropic raised $81.3B in the largest-ever stock market debut Thursday, briefly driving the Claude maker’s valuation north of $2T and delivering a vote of confidence for an artificial intelligence infrastructure boom that has faced growing scrutiny from investors. Wikimedia Commons/TechCrunch Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei in 2023 Shares began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market at $111.50 and climbed as high as $114.99 midday Thursday before dipping back below $100 — but still well above the company’s $83 offering price and the $70-to-$78 range Anthropic had anticipated earlier this month. The debut surpasses the previous initial public offering record set by rival AI firm SpaceX in June. The offering comes at a turbulent moment for the AI trade and the data center and digital infrastructure sector supporting it. Investors have grown increasingly uneasy about the staggering sums tech giants are spending to fund an infrastructure construction boom that has yet to generate commensurate returns. Rising community opposition and political headwinds in the wake of this month’s midterm elections have added another layer of uncertainty. The anxiety has been felt in public markets, with several companies tied closely to the AI data center boom delaying planned IPOs in recent weeks amid concerns about valuations and investor appetite for AI. Anthropic's debut may provide a counterpoint to that narrative and a direct boost to the data center sector. The IPO gives one of the world’s largest AI labs a massive pool of capital, a significant portion of which will flow toward computing capacity and data centers. Bryn Talkington, managing partner of Requisite Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday that Anthropic becoming a public company also provides transparency into a major demand driver for digital infrastructure that has previously been lacking. This could give investors confidence that tech’s AI infrastructure spending spree will deliver returns. “This raise solidifies the capex spend,” Talkington said. “Now you have a real player that’s not being marked up by VC companies. You have a real player — SEC, quarterly earnings — and that creates transparency and accountability, which I think is a wonderful thing.” Anthropic’s move to the public markets coincides with a strategic shift that is expected to make the firm a major player in the data center landscape. In its S-1 prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in October, Anthropic disclosed plans to reduce its reliance on cloud providers by leasing dedicated data centers at significant scale and operating its own computing hardware inside them. The strategy marks a departure for a company that has previously relied almost entirely on cloud providers like Amazon , Google and Microsoft for its computing power. Through the initiative, Anthropic Direct, leased data centers under Anthropic’s control will account for a growing share of the $542B to $567B the company plans to spend on computing infrastructure in the coming years, it said in the S-1 filing. Anthropic doesn't intend to develop data centers itself. Third-party providers will secure land and power, build facilities to Anthropic’s specifications and operate them on its behalf. The initiative is already moving beyond the planning stage, with Anthropic entering into purchase and lease agreements for Anthropic Direct, according to its SEC filing. “As our compute requirements have scaled, we have transitioned to a hybrid model in which, in addition to purchasing compute as a cloud service, we also procure specialized AI accelerators directly and operate this hardware in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification,” the company wrote in its SEC filing. But the company also said in its SEC filing that challenges building data centers will present a risk for the company, and the headwinds facing data center development have only increased since. November’s midterms saw voters across the U.S. approve local moratoriums and other measures to restrict data center development, while elections in key markets like Texas and Georgia produced new governors and other state officials who campaigned on limiting data centers. Democratic control of both chambers of Congress is also expected to bring greater scrutiny for the industry. Speaking with CNBC on Thursday morning, Anthropic President Daniela Amodei said the company will prioritize local input in its data center build-out to ensure communities don’t feel that the technology “is happening to them.” She also said the company is committed to paying for any increases in the cost of grid power that may occur due to the firm’s data centers. “From our perspective, building data centers is something where we also need to listen to what it is that those communities want and help to bring forward that future as well,” she said, adding that the company is aiming to “make sure that any cost increase is not borne by the consumer.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Anthropic , Artificial Intelligence , Claude , Dario Amodei , NASDAQ

items.title: Office REIT Sells Reston Property To Local Firm For 30% Of 2014 Price
items.description: Office Properties Income Trust, which emerged from bankruptcy in June, has offloaded a Reston, Virginia, office building for less than a third of its sale price 12 years ago. Google Maps The 135K SF office property at 1775 Wiehle Ave. in Reston, Virginia The REIT, managed by Massachusetts-based The RMR Group, sold the 135K SF property at 1775 Wiehle Ave. — which is just over half vacant — to Bethesda-based Polinger Co. for $12.1M. The sale closed Oct. 22, according to Fairfax County property records. That price is well below what it sold for in 2014, when First Potomac Realty Trust paid $41M for the asset. OPI gained control of the property three years later, when it acquired First Potomac. Polinger likes the supply-and-demand dynamics of the Reston office market, with growing appetite from defense and technology companies and a tightening supply as office parks are converted to residential, John Gordon, president of the firm's development arm, told Bisnow . "We think over the years that the value goes up tremendously because of the lack of new buildings and taking down the buildings and just this great location," he said. OPI did not respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for RMR declined to comment on its behalf. OPI is selling off large swaths of its now 16M SF office portfolio. The REIT, like many other office-heavy owners, was hit hard by post-pandemic tidal shifts in office capital markets. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October 2025, a year after notifying investors about doubts that it could continue operating in light of its maturing debt. During the restructuring process, OPI shed $714M in debt, leaving it with $1.7B in money owed. At the end of its restructuring, it said it had 31 properties totaling 3M SF on the market that it would sell to repay debts. As of the end of September, the REIT was under agreements to sell 15 office assets totaling more than 1.7M SF, according to its third-quarter report , including one more in Reston and two in Washington, D.C. OPI already sold 13 properties, totaling 1.5M SF, during the third quarter. Those were sold for a total of $143M, and OPI recorded a $5.5M loss on the sales. One of those sales was a 140K SF Dupont Circle office building, which it offloaded for $6.2M in September. On the 1775 Wiehle sale, OPI recorded a $2.3M loss on impairment of real estate. 1775 Wiehle, which was built in 2000, is just under 50% leased, Gordon told Bisnow . The building is anchored by law firm Odin Feldman Pittleman, which has a 35K SF long-term lease at the property, he said. Other tenants include law firm Goel & Anderson and Forge Financial Group. Polinger plans to put money into tenant improvement allowances and build out a full floor of spec suites, in addition to a spec-suite floor added by OPI. The company is seeing interest from medical tenants as well as engineering companies and government contracting firms, Gordon said. Polinger’s website says it manages 3M SF of office, retail and mixed-use space across the D.C. area, including office buildings in the District, Fairfax, Bethesda, Chevy Chase, Gaithersburg and Landover. This summer, the company offloaded a 235K SF Navy Yard office building to Matthew Jemal’s new investment firm, Jemal Equities. The $193.3M price for 99 M St. SE was 43% less than Polinger paid when it bought the property in 2019. For 1775 Wiehle, Newmark represented both sides of the transaction, Kassandra Saridakis, a capital markets managing director for the brokerage, told Bisnow. Jud Ryan, James Cassidy and Grant Marley represented the seller. Saridakis worked with Joe Donato, Andrew Asbill and Kevin Ridgway to arrange acquisition financing for Polinger. items.title: Brookfield Bets $110M On Resorts Company Rolling Up Independent Campgrounds
items.description: Unsplash/Andre Ouellet Brookfield Asset Management plans to spend $110M to buy a minority stake in a company that is buying up independent campgrounds with the expectation that the pandemic-era recreation boom is more than a fleeting trend. BAM is getting into business with Open Road Resorts, which has campgrounds across the country, including near Yellowstone National Park and in New York’s Finger Lakes region, Bloomberg reported . Open Road will use the money to acquire more campgrounds. The properties usually have RV sites as well as glamping tents and full-season sites for campers looking to post up for extended stays. Luxury RV campgrounds made up roughly 20% of the outdoor hospitality industry last year. The business was valued then at between $8B and $9B but received such heavy investment that it was expected to grow up to $30B in the next five years, Bisnow previously reported . Open Road was founded in 2019. In 2024, it raised capital from firms including consumer product investor L Catterton and recreational vehicle-maker Thor Industries Inc. to acquire RV parks, upgrade facilities and improve booking and revenue management systems. The changing demographics of RV owners, now skewing younger and wealthier, have fueled the push for upgrades and added amenities at RV parks. Brookfield and other institutional investors have placed money in more nontraditional real estate assets as the market has changed since the pandemic. Aside from campgrounds, firms are buying marinas and have plowed billions into industrial outdoor storage . items.title: Developer Plans 595 Apartments At Woburn Transit Center
items.description: A plan is moving forward to build hundreds of housing units on a 6-acre site at the Anderson Regional Transportation Center in Woburn. Wikimedia Commons/Pi.1415926535 An aerial view of the Anderson Regional Transportation Center Boston-based developer Cabot, Cabot & Forbes was the sole respondent to Massport 's request for the site, proposing a 595-unit project, Banker & Tradesman first reported . The Massport board of directors unanimously backed the developer's proposal during a Thursday morning meeting. The transportation center includes stops on the MBTA commuter rail's Lowell line and the Amtrak Downeaster line to Maine, and it offers direct bus service to the airport through Logan Express. The site includes nearly 2,400 parking spaces and sits in a 260-acre Superfund site that has contaminants from centuries-old manufacturing. Massport, in partnership with the Massachusetts Department of Transportation and the MBTA, issued a request for expressions of interest in February 2025 to gauge the site's "potential for commercial and residential development to co-exist with, and even enhance, operations at the facility." The project needs approval from all three agencies to move forward. CCF will then need to obtain zoning approval from the city and the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act Office. CCF has developed another 389-unit project in the Superfund site: The Point at Woburn at 120 Commerce Way. The developer also celebrated the topping off of The Bolt , a 180K SF manufacturing facility on New Boston Street. And Cabot, Cabot & Forbes has proposed another multifamily project called Zero New Boston , a seven-story, 250-apartment complex planned to be built at 0 New Boston St. next to the transportation center. CCF said it has invested roughly $400M in the site. Woburn officials have been trying to reimagine the New Boston Street corridor , hiring RKG Associates to conduct a study on redevelopment and reinvestment opportunities. As part of a March presentation, the city explored several options for reinvestment , including a mixed-use district and a modified industrial zone. items.title: Why housing construction is sliding back toward COVID-era lows
items.description: The great housing construction boom that people have been cheering about for four years now looks to be on the cusp of falling to COVID-era lows. How is this possible when people have been saying for the past five years that we need to build more homes and Congress just passed the giant ROAD to Housing Act this summer — which was designed to help spur more construction. The old laws of economics still play out here; there simply isn’t enough housing demand to build more homes. This is something I wrote about back in June 2021 : when mortgage rates eventually rise this whole thing will reverse. Now, in November 2026, we are not that far away from the COVID-19 recession lows, as housing permits are already at COVID-19 recession levels and mortgage rates are above 7%. Building permits From Census : Building Permits: Privately-owned housing units authorized by building permits in October were at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1,295,000. This is 7.4 percent below the revised September rate of 1,398,000 and is 8.7 percent below the October 2025 rate of 1,418,000. Single-family authorizations in October were at a rate of 772,000; this is 8.7 percent below the revised September figure of 846,000. Authorizations of units in buildings with five units or more were at a rate of 475,000 in October. As we can see in the chart below, housing permits have been slowly falling for years and we are not only at levels last seen during the COVID-19 recession, but we’re on pace to hit the lows of that time period if this trend continues. And all this is happening when mortgage rates are close to 7.5% and the Fed is starting a new rate hike cycle. Single-family permits are not only close to the lows of 2022, but not that far from the COVID-19 recession lows either. Builders have done an admirable job keeping new home sales elevated enough to keep housing starts from falling further, but that has limits as profit margins fall. As you can see here, the single-family permits have taken a noticeable dive. Builders confidence at multiyear lows One question I got recently, which has merit: Why is builder confidence at multiyear lows, but new home sales have grown over the last few months? Just remember that the builder confidence index is tilted toward smaller homebuilders, not the big publicly traded homebuilders that are still buying down rates to move product. New home sales are still at 2019 levels, and so are housing starts and permits. If the big builders lose their ability to buy down rates, this sales data should eventually break below 2019 levels, but for now sales have operated within a small range for the past 10 years. Conclusion Since mortgage rates shot toward 7.60%, we have seen housing data turn very negative. Compare that to last year at this time, when mortgage rates were heading toward 6% and existing home sales hit a nine-month high. The big builders can only do so much to keep starts from falling more. For now, it doesn’t look good for housing construction in 2027, given where mortgage rates are at and the builders profit margins falling more and more. Related More:

items.title: Dakota Fanning Cleaned Up After Sister Elle While Living and Making Their First Film Together as Co-Stars: ‘Like a Tornado Has Run Through’
items.description: Elle and Dakota Fanning have been in the spotlight for decades, but their upcoming project, “The Nightingale,” marks the first time they’ve played sisters onscreen —an experience that brought them “closer” together, both on set and at home. While they’ve visited each other on set in the past and even separately played different versions of the same character in the 2001 film “I Am Sam,” Elle, 28, told Vanity Fair that actually working with each other is a totally different ball game. “It certainly brought us closer, which was hard to imagine—to be closer,” she said. “Our mom always left us little notes in suitcases, like, ‘Just savor this time together. This is precious.’” Dakota, 32, confirmed that they took their mother’s advice. “We did really savor it,” she said. “And the biggest takeaway for me is when we have each other and when we’re together, we can do anything. That’s really how I feel. There’s nothing that I couldn’t do with Elle there with me.” Loading... Real-life sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning will play siblings on screen for the first time, an experience that brought them much closer together. Taylor Hill/FilmMagic Loading... They lived together while filming in Hungary, and Dakota said she spent lots of time cleaning up after Elle. Jean Catuffe/GC Images That said, the job wasn’t easy. The Fannings traveled to Budapest to shoot on location , where they lived together. “It was a challenging shoot, not going to lie. It was physically tiring, certainly emotionally taxing,” said Elle. After a long day of using lots of “brain power” on set, the sisters had to find a way to “recharge” each evening. For Dakota and Elle, that meant eating lots of Thai food and streaming “The Real Housewives,” true crime, and “Margo’s Got Money Troubles”—the TV series the younger sister stars in, which was released while they filmed “The Nightingale.” Dakota revealed that on a day off, she’d often find herself cleaning up after Elle, which was poetic as her character, Vianne, also tidies her sister Isabelle’s mess. “Her bed in the mornings is like a tornado has run through it,” she said. “She’s just one of those sleepers. It’s all twisted into a crazy thing. I was like, ‘That’s no fun to get into a bed that’s all crumpled and rumpled. Let me make it nice.’” The older sister said that “it became a routine,” and she “always made her bed like that” when possible. Elle said, “It’s art imitating life, because there’s even a scene where Vianne is making Isabelle’s bed, too.” Dakota and Elle were born in Conyers, GA . As young girls, they traveled between the Atlanta suburb and Los Angeles to work before relocating to the West Coast full time. Loading... Elle has said that it's been "fulfilling to merge" their lives as adults, after trying to stay separate as children. Dominique Charriau/Getty Images Loading... The sisters even purchased a house together in 2017, where they lived together until they offloaded it about three years later. items.title: The Ultimate Playbook To Buying a Home Without 20% Down Using Grants and Assistance Programs
items.description: Buying a home can be an intimidating process, with the biggest hurdle for many being coming up with enough funds for a down payment . Many people believe they need to put down at least 20% if they want a home. But that's not necessarily true. Most buyers have down payments ranging from 3.5% to 20% of the sale price of the home they're buying, and there are many down payment assistance programs that can help aspiring homeowners pivot from home browser to homebuyer. These programs can help buyers snag a home by providing cash that can go toward a down payment. There are even loan programs for certain qualified buyers that don't require any down payments. The array of offerings from federal, local, and private sources can take the form of looser loan requirements, outright grants of money, or tax credits, all of which make homeownership more affordable. First-time homebuyers , often with certain qualifications, are often beneficiaries of the assistance. Lower-income buyers, those who serve in the military or are veterans, and those who purchase fixer-uppers or homes in rural areas might also be eligible for the help. The assistance ranges greatly, from a grant of several thousand dollars to, at the high end, a savings of five figures over the life of the loan . What are down payment assistance programs? Down payment assistance can take several forms and can even help buyers circumvent the PMI payment. While 20% down has been something of a gold standard for homebuyers, it's also the minimum that generally lets them avoid private mortgage insurance , or PMI, which is assessed because lenders believe the loan carries risk. This in turn raises the homebuyer’s monthly expenses. Here's an example: PMI is typically 0.5% to 1% of the loan amount per year. So if buyers put down less than 20% and their mortgage is $300,000, their PMI would be between $1,500 and $3,000 per year. That would add about $125 to $250 per month on top of their mortgage payment, a significant charge. (Homeowners can have PMI canceled when the equity in their home surpasses 20%.) So, while a buyer can also choose loans that require a down payment of just a single digit, that PMI can stretch a budget paper-thin. That's where down payment assistance can help. At least 2,000 such programs exist across the country. Some are federal, but most tend to be at state and local levels, which is important to know when searching for help. Private organizations, from lenders to nonprofits, also work with borrowers who need help. These programs might offer grants, loans, tax credits, or a combination of a couple of these benefits. Funding can come from our government, nonprofits, and private enterprises. Let’s take a closer look: Grants might be the most desirable form of down payment assistance. Typically, a grant is fully forgiven at closing and never has to be paid back. Yes, we’re talking about free money! About 7% of down payment help comes in the form of grants, says Veronica Khandelwal , vice president of HFA Relations at Down Payment Resource , which provides consumers with guidance on this kind of assistance. But there is a catch. “Grants require owner occupancy," she says of the requirement for buyers to live in these properties. That's to make sure these loans don't go to investors or vacation-home buyers. "Some programs allow grants to be applied to multifamily purchases of one to four units so long as one of the units is occupied by the borrower." Loading... Forgivable loans are another option. These loans need to be repaid only if a repayment trigger event occurs, such as the home being sold before the end of the term, the home being no longer owner-occupied, the title being transferred, or the loan being defaulted on. Deferred-payment loans are also available. These are paid back either at the end of the loan term or if a repayment trigger occurs. So, while it’s not a gift, it will help homebuyers get over that down payment hurdle and buy a house they might otherwise not have been able to afford. Repayable loans are another leg up on homeownership. They require borrowers to make monthly payments, like a typical loan. But here's the good part: They do so at interest rates starting as low as 0%. That helps spread the down payment and closing costs over a number of years, making it much easier to enter the housing market. Some agencies also offer a combination of these forms of assistance. That could mean that a portion of the help will be forgiven (or “written off” with no repayment needed), while some will need to be repaid. Tax credits are sometimes offered as well, further sweetening the deal. Each down payment assistance program will have its own rules and guidelines, but the vast majority are offered only for a home that buyers will live in as a primary residence. The best first-time home buyer programs in 2026 Here are some of the more popular national options folks might access to help them to pivot from home shopper to homebuyer. FHA (Federal Housing Authority) loans were created by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for first-time homeowners (HUD). These mortgages allow as little as 3.5% for the down payment, provided buyers have a credit score of 580 or higher, along with other qualifying factors. The federal government insures these loans, and for that reason, banks are more willing to loan money to homebuyers who have neither top-tier credit nor loads of cash to put down on the purchase. FHA Section 203(k) loans require only 3% down, provided qualifying buyers will live in the property, typically one that needs work, while they fix it up. For buyers hoping for a DIY route into a dream home, this could be a win-win. The cost of improvements is included in the loan so buyers can finance both the home and up to $35,000 in repairs. items.description: Perez Hilton has returned to his Miami residence after a health incident left him hospitalized . The 48-year-old was hospitalized in August following a distressing livestream that prompted several calls to police and requests for a welfare check. items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs. Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 11/19/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.28% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.66% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Average 7.28% While prospective borrowers often shop around for a home, they may not always think to do the same for their mortgage, as comparing multiple rate quotes can potentially save them thousands over a loan’s lifetime. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.28% as of November 19, 2026, up from last week when it averaged 7.11%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.26%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.66%, up from last week when it averaged 6.45%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.54%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% YOY decrease in properties sold. NYC Capital Markets: Volume Moderates but Remains on Track for Recovery Year After four quarters of sustained recovery, investment sales slowed in the third quarter. Dollar volume totaled $5.6 billion, a 30.7% quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) decline and the first quarter since Q2 2025 to fall short of at least $8.0 billion. Investor confidence, which had steadily improved over the last year, was tempered by rising interest rates, uncertainty around the broader economy and geopolitical conditions, and the historically consistent trend of an election cycle pause. Despite the slowdown, the year-to-date (YTD) dollar volume total of $22.0 billion remains virtually unchanged from the same period last year, while the year’s annualized pace of $29.3 billion would represent a 23.3% increase over the 2020 cyclical low. In Q3 2026, there were 517 transactions involving the sale of 578 properties—an 18.2% year-over-year (YOY) decrease in properties sold. Average pricing for core property types across New York City fell to $504 per square foot (psf), a 0.6% decrease from the 2025 average. Cap rates for core property types have continued to inch higher in 2026 and now stand at an average of 7.13%. Sector Highlights Office: Dollar volume in Q3 2026 dipped to $1.4 billion, bringing the YTD total to $5.5 billion, only 7.8% below the same period last year. Although activity remains muted compared to historical levels, the investor pool is steadily expanding, with deals this quarter completed by a diverse mix of institutional, REIT, private capital, and user-purchasers. The average deal size declined for the third consecutive quarter, to $46.8 million, as smaller private capital players deployed more capital into value-add strategies for discounted and underutilized assets. At the same time, larger investors remain attracted to well-positioned, sizeable Class A assets with favorable tenancy and capital improvement conditions. Pricing has declined nominally this year, down 4.2% to $478 psf. Multifamily: Although combined dollar volume for elevator and walk-up properties slowed to $1.1 billion in Q3 2026, the YTD total of $4.8 billion falls only 11.7% short of the total from the same period last year, which marked the strongest year since 2022. Similar to the office sector, multifamily demand is starkly bifurcated between market-rate, newly-constructed, often luxury assets versus majority-rent-regulated, deeply discounted offerings—though both segments are exhibiting encouraging momentum. Substantial renter demand has kept vacancy at historic lows and attracted a growing pool of capital from both core/core-plus investors as well as value-add players. Development: Volume pulled back slightly to $831.6 million in Q3 2026, but the sector remains on pace to finish at $5.0 billion: if achieved, 2026 and 2025 would be the only two years since 2019 to surpass that benchmark. Depressed land values and a still-limited supply pipeline continued to drive activity. That momentum, previously focused in Manhattan, has begun to spread to the city’s secondary markets: four out of the five largest development transactions this quarter were located in the Outer Boroughs, totaling $249.6 million across 1.3 million buildable square feet. Increased demand has continued to support pricing recovery, with the citywide price per buildable square foot rising 6.4% YOY to $227, the highest average since 2019. Core retail sales grew 5.5%, with underlying volumes increasing 2.8%, signaling stronger consumer demand as the holiday shopping quarter began. Gas station sales surged 30.1%, contributing to overall sales growth, while early holiday promotions helped lift non-store sales by 10.1%. Apparel continued to attract shoppers seeking value and seasonal purchases. Apparel sales increased 4.9%, with underlying volumes rising 1.2% as consumers favored discounted mid- and premium-priced merchandise. Clothing foot traffic climbed 6.4%, while department store visits jumped 11.3%, highlighting strong in-store engagement ahead of the holidays. Electronics spending remained strong, with sales increasing 7.6% despite a 3.4% decline in store visits. Product innovation and replacement demand helped support spending, even as consumers became more selective about where and how they shop. Furniture and furnishings sales rose 2.2%, with foot traffic increasing 2.1%, suggesting gradual improvement in home-related spending despite ongoing housing market challenges. Experiences and hobbies continued to draw consumers. Theater and music venue visits surged 28.5%, attractions increased 11.4%, and hobbies, gifts and crafts traffic climbed 17.9%. Meanwhile, grocery sales grew just 1.2%, with underlying volumes declining 0.5%, reflecting continued pressure on household budgets and a shift toward value-oriented shopping channels. items.title: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012
items.description: Home Purchase Loans Fall to Lowest Third-Quarter Level Since 2012 by ATTOM Team | Nov 19, 2026 | Mortgage Origination , Real Estate News - Recent Articles Home purchase lending falls 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans; Refinance lending drops 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans IRVINE, Calif. – Nov. 19, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, today released its U.S. Residential Property Mortgage Origination Report for the third quarter of 2026, showing purchase and refinance lending slowed from the previous quarter as mortgage rates climbed and home purchase loans fell to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012. A total of 1.29 million purchase and refinance mortgages secured by residential property (1 to 4 units) were originated in the third quarter, down 12 percent from the previous quarter and 15 percent from a year earlier. Total loan volume reached $498.1 billion, down 15 percent quarterly and 12 percent year-over-year. The quarterly slowdown was driven by declines in both home purchase and refinance lending. Purchase loans fell 9 percent from the previous quarter to 729,968, marking the lowest third-quarter total since 2012. Purchase loans were down 12 percent from a year earlier, even as the average purchase loan amount rose 3 percent over the same period to $411,756. “The increase in refinance activity we saw late last year and into early this year cooled in the third quarter, with refinancing declining more than purchase lending,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “Purchase loans also slipped to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as higher mortgage rates and elevated average purchase loan amounts continued to strain affordability for many buyers.” Purchase lending slips quarterly in most markets Purchase lending totaled $300.6 billion in the third quarter, down 10 percent from the previous quarter and 10 percent below year-ago levels. Purchase loans accounted for 56.5 percent of all purchase and refinance originations, up from 54.5 percent in both the second quarter of 2026 and the third quarter of 2025. Purchase activity declined quarterly in 73.6 percent of analyzed metro areas with a population of 200,000 or more and sufficient data. Among metros with populations above 1 million, the largest quarterly increases were in Buffalo, NY (up 61 percent); Memphis, TN (up 50 percent); Rochester, NY (up 32 percent); New York, NY (up 22 percent); and Hartford, CT (up 20 percent). The steepest quarterly drops among large metros were in Salt Lake City, UT; New Orleans, LA; Denver, CO; Atlanta, GA; and Richmond, VA. Refinancing activity falls sharply quarter-over-quarter Refinancing activity fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans, the lowest quarterly total since the second quarter of 2024, and was 19 percent below the third quarter of 2025. Refinance originations accounted for 43.5 percent of all purchase and refinance loans, down from 45.5 percent in both the previous quarter and a year earlier. Refinance lending declined quarterly in 89.4 percent of analyzed metro areas, with the steepest quarterly drops among large metros in San Jose, CA; Dallas, TX; San Francisco, CA; Austin, TX; and Louisville, KY. FHA and VA loan shares decline quarterly Loans backed by the Federal Housing Administration accounted for 15.7 percent of all purchase and refinance originations in the third quarter, down from 16.1 percent in the second quarter and 17.9 percent a year earlier. VA-backed loans represented 6.9 percent of originations, down from 8.2 percent in the second quarter and 7.2 percent a year earlier, the lowest share since the second quarter of 2024. Mortgage rates climb above 7 percent by early October Mortgage rates trended higher during the quarter. According to Freddie Mac, the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage rose from 6.43 percent in early July to 7.28 percent by early October, adding pressure to an already constrained housing market. Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Loan Origination Report key takeaways According to the Q3 2026 Loan Origination Report, purchase and refinance lending slowed in the third quarter of 2026, with originations falling 12 percent from the previous quarter to 1.29 million loans as mortgage rates climbed above 7 percent. Home purchase lending dropped 9 percent quarter-over-quarter to 729,968 loans, the lowest third-quarter level since 2012, while refinance lending fell 16 percent quarter-over-quarter to 561,290 loans. Report methodology ATTOM analyzed recorded mortgage and deed of trust data for single-family homes, condos, town homes and multi-family properties of two to four units for this report. This report covers purchase and refinance loan originations. Each recorded mortgage or deed of trust was counted as a separate loan origination. Dollar volume was calculated by multiplying the total number of loan originations by the average loan amount for those loan originations.
